core.text: Latin verse runs not on rhyme but on **the metre (the rhythm of a line: the hexameter and pentameter of the elegiac couplet, Catullus's eleven-syllable line)** — a fixed pattern of long (–) and short (⏑) syllables (the prosody lesson says which). Syllables group into feet: a dactyl (– ⏑ ⏑, *fē-mi-na*) or a spondee (– –, *nē-mō*). Latin name: *versus: hexameter, pentameter, hendecasyllabus*.
Like *DUM-da-da DUM-da-da* in a limerick: the beat is the pattern, the words must fit it. 'Long' means takes longer to say, not louder.

Hexameter: six feet of dactyls or spondees, fifth nearly always a dactyl, sixth two syllables. Pentameter: two halves of two and a half feet with a break (||), the second half always dactyl, dactyl, syllable. Hexameter + pentameter = elegiac couplet.

core.text: Ovid (Week 13): *Nōn ego | nōbili|um sede|ō studi|ōsus e|quōrum* — five dactyls, spondee; *cui tamen | ipsa fa|vēs || vincat ut | ille pre|cor* — dactyl, dactyl, half, twice. *um* is long before *s*; *sus* stays short.
Metre is the pattern to fill; prosody is the rules for syllable length and swallowed vowels. Mark syllables first, then divide into feet.

more.text: Martial's couplet (Week 14) scanned: *Nōn amo | tē, Sabi|dī, nec | possum | dīcere | quārē* — dactyl, dactyl, spondee, spondee, dactyl, spondee; *Hoc tan|tum pos|sum || dīcere | nōn amo | tē* — spondee, spondee, half; dactyl, dactyl, half. Twice the final *-ō* of *amō* is counted short, a licence Ørberg notes (*volŏ, nēmŏ*); *nec* and *Hoc* are long because a consonant follows.

Ørberg's chapter 34 (*Dē versibus*) explains the names: the hexameter from Greek *hex*, six, because it has six feet, five dactyls (spondees may replace them, but the fifth is always a dactyl) and a final spondee or trochee (– ⏑); the pentameter from *pente*, five, because its two halves of two and a half feet make five, and the second half admits no spondees; a pentameter always follows a hexameter. The break in the middle of a pentameter, and the word-break usually found in the third foot of a hexameter (*Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, || nec possum*), is the caesura, the natural pause when reading aloud.

Catullus's hendecasyllable (Greek *hendeka*, eleven) has eleven syllables in five feet: spondee, dactyl, trochee, trochee, spondee or trochee — *Vīvā|mus mea | Lesbi(a) | atqu(e) a|mēmus*; *Passer | mortuu(s) | est me|ae pu|ellae*; *Cēnā|bis bene | mī Fa|bull(e) a|pud mē*. Its first foot is occasionally an iamb (⏑ –) or a trochee. Ovid wrote the *Amōrēs* in couplets; Martial's epigrams use both the couplet and the hendecasyllable.

sources: Ørberg cap. XXXIV Grammatica Latina (Dē versibus)
